idiom_name: master coordinator + homogeneous worker pool over a shared task queue
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one coordinator decomposes the input into independent work items and publishes them on a shared queue; a fixed set of workers repeatedly take one item, compute a partial result in isolation and publish it back; the coordinator collects every result (or its failure), combines them into the final answer and then stops the workers. The decomposition, the queue discipline (pull versus push versus work-stealing), the concurrency bound and the aggregation order are the real design decisions; the workers themselves stay interchangeable and task-agnostic. Shutdown is explicit - a sentinel or poison pill, a closed queue, or cooperative cancellation - and a worker must never wait for another worker's result.
code_sketch:
master:
    items = decompose(input)
    publish(items)                      # shared queue, bounded
    partials = [collect result or failure for each item]
    total = combine(partials)
    stop_workers()                      # sentinel / close queue / cancel
worker:
    loop: item = queue.take(); publish(compute(item))
pitfalls: Letting the coordinator also execute work items turns it into the bottleneck and hides the achievable parallelism.
A shared queue without a bound or back-pressure grows without limit, while per-worker queues skew the load.
Without an explicit stop signal and a join, workers outlive the master or block forever on an empty queue.
Unbounded result collection without a timeout leaves the master waiting indefinitely for a dead worker.
Failing to make tasks idempotent allows duplicate execution when a worker is falsely presumed dead and its tasks reassigned.
Thundering herd: releasing all workers simultaneously after a queue lull floods the system with requests.
Memory blowup from accumulating large Future/Task objects without consuming results: always drain the result stream concurrently with dispatch.
Head-of-line blocking on FIFO queue: a slow task at the front stalls all subsequent tasks in the same per-worker queue.

Wrong move: build a custom master for partition ownership when Kafka consumer groups or an existing queue already coordinate consumers -> heartbeat races and split-brain reassignments cause duplicate execution -> instead use the broker's coordinator and make handlers idempotent.

Wrong move: submit remote microtasks without a concurrency or queue bound -> serialization, pending-result memory, and downstream overload erase parallel speedup -> instead cap in-flight work, propagate back-pressure, and coarsen partitions.

Wrong move: use remote partitioning to hide a CPU-bound microtask bottleneck -> messaging and process-boundary overhead dominates item processing -> instead use local parallelism or larger partitions, reserving remote partitioning for I/O-bound steps.
